# Dealing with values the microscope cannot see {#sec-missing-data-measurement-error}















I have a spreadsheet row that I have looked at more often than I should. It is mouse KO86, in the hanging wire test of @sec-beta-robust-regression, and 7 of its nine attempts say the same thing: *60 seconds*. The next two mice on the list, KO10 and KO105, have 5 and 5 of nine. Sixty seconds is not what those mice did. It is where the test stops: the experimenter takes the animal off the wire, the clock stops, and the row says 60. **How long would they have taken, if we had let them hang?** Nobody knows. What we know is that it was *more than 60*.

In earlier chapters I did the sensible-looking thing with those attempts and told you, each time, that I was not proud of it: I dropped them. The chapter on behavior (@sec-beta-robust-regression) modeled the completed crossing times only, the chapter on varying slopes (@sec-multilevel-varying-slopes) did the same, and the chapter on multilevel GLMs (@sec-multilevel-glmm) repaired the independence problem and left this one standing. Each time I wrote that the principled repair was a censored model and that it was a topic for this chapter. This is the chapter, and the first half of it pays that debt.

The second half is about values that are missing for other reasons. The chapters of this part set aside sections of brains that never made it into the file (@sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts), open-field sessions in which the tracker lost the mouse (@sec-longitudinal-timeseries), and a count whose error I mentioned and did not model (@sec-multivariate-distributional-regression). They are not the same problem as the 60-second cap, and I want to convince you that telling them apart is most of the work. @fig-mdme_attempts starts with the wire, because it is the case in which the missing values are on the page.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
  geom_jitter(width = 0.22, height = 0, size = 1.9, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~genotype, labeller = labeller(genotype = c(WT = "Control", KO = "Klf4-KO"))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_end) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Crossed" = 16, "Reached the cap" = 17, "Fell" = 4)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3) +
  labs(x = "Training day", y = "Time on the wire (s)", color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_top()
```

I drew @fig-mdme_attempts with `ggplot2::geom_jitter()`, one mark per attempt, because with 567 attempts there is no reason to summarize before looking. A bar of mean crossing time per genotype, with asterisks, would be computed from the grey circles only (if you drop the rest) or would average the cap into the times as if the mice had really crossed at 60 (if you keep it), and in both cases it would hide the thing that is plainly visible here: a row of orange triangles that is a few marks long on the left and a crowd on the right, on every day. The design tip is to show *how each value ended*, not only its number, whenever a column mixes measurements with something else. Shape and color carry the same information, so it also reads in a grayscale print.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read the grey circles first: that is the part of the experiment that produced a time. Then find the dotted line and count the orange triangles sitting on it; they are not times, they are the places where we stopped looking. Compare the two panels *by the length of the row of triangles*, not by where the circles are, and notice that the row is longer on the right on all three days. Last, find the black crosses: they are a different event (a fall), and they are not triangles that happen to be early. The mistake to avoid is to read the height of an orange triangle as a measurement.
:::

## Three ways of not having the number {#sec-mdme-kinds}

There are, I think, three different reasons a number is not in your spreadsheet, and the habit I want you to leave with is asking *which one is it?* before touching any code. I picture them as three jars on a bench. In the first, the number is **absent**: the section was lost, the tracker lost the mouse, the animal did not survive the surgery. Something that could have been measured was not. In the second, the number is **hidden behind a limit**: the mouse was still hanging at 60 seconds, a western blot band is brighter than the film can record, a qPCR reaction did not cross the threshold. A measurement exists, and what we got back is only that it lies beyond a point. In the third, the number is **blurred**: the count of NeuN-positive cells in a region came from a microscope and a counting rule, and it carries a counting error that the spreadsheet does not show.

In the second, a ruler that disappears into fog: a number that is only known to be beyond a point. In the third, a line drawn twice with a shaky hand: a number that is there, with some smear around it.](images/missing-data-measurement-error_three-jars.png){#fig-mdme-jars fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of three glass jars with cork lids on a wooden shelf. The first holds teal and ochre jigsaw pieces with one white gap among them. The second holds a wooden ruler standing upright whose marks are clear in the lower half and fade into pale teal fog above. The third holds a sheet with a teal line and an ochre line drawn side by side with a soft ochre smudge between them."}

@fig-mdme-jars is the map of the chapter: the first jar holds the number that is absent, the second the one hidden behind a limit and the third the one that is blurred, and the sections that follow take them in the order hidden, absent and blurred.

The three jars need different handling, and treating them alike is the commonest mistake I know. An absent value should be handled by asking why it is absent and by using a model that does not need it (or by saying what you assumed about it). A hidden value should *stay in the model*, with what we know about it, which is that it is beyond the limit. A blurred value should be modeled with its blur, which for a count has a known size. @tbl-mdme_kinds puts the three side by side with the case in this book that stands for each.






::: {#tbl-mdme_kinds .cell tbl-cap='Three ways of not having the number, what each assumes and what each costs, with the case of this chapter that stands for each one.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
                     "That the value is at least (or at most) a limit",

  `Tempting shortcut` = c("Drop the unit, or fill it with the group mean",

                          "Treat the value as exact"),
  `What the shortcut costs` = c("Biased if the loss depends on the value; the lost units are not a random sample",

                                "Nothing if the error is small; attenuation and false precision if it is not"),
  `Better` = c("A model that uses what exists, and a sensitivity analysis for what cannot be checked",
               "A censored likelihood: the value contributes the probability of being beyond the limit",

  `Case in this chapter` = c("Open-field sessions, NeuN sections, one PDGFR-beta count",
```

Notice that the second row of @tbl-mdme_kinds is the one most scientists meet first and handle worst. A value below the limit of detection of an assay is replaced by half the limit, a time that reached the cap is entered as the cap, a band that saturated is entered at its maximum. Every one of those is a small act of invention, and the textbooks that this book follows are unanimous about it: dropping censored observations gives the wrong estimate, because what you drop is not a random subset, and substituting a constant creates a spike of identical values that shrinks the spread and distorts the slope [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. A reader of @sec-eda-missing-data will recognize the structure; this chapter is where the idea meets its second and third kinds.

## The mechanisms, on one page {#sec-mdme-mechanisms}

The vocabulary for absent values is the one of @sec-eda-missing-data, and I do not repeat the simulation that showed what each mechanism does to an estimate. I only need the three letters to be at hand. @tbl-mdme_mechanisms puts them next to the real cases of this chapter, and then I use the table for the rest of the chapter.






::: {#tbl-mdme_mechanisms .cell tbl-cap='The three missingness mechanisms of the earlier chapter, what a model that uses all the available data assumes under each, and the case of this chapter that I would place under it. The last column is a judgment from what I know of the experiments, not something the data can show.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Mechanisms, what a likelihood-based analysis of the available data assumes, and the examples
mech <- data.frame(
  Mechanism = c("Missing completely at random (MCAR)", "Missing at random (MAR)", "Missing not at random (MNAR)"),
  `What it says` = c("The chance of being missing is unrelated to anything",
                     "The chance depends only on what is in the model (group, day, earlier values)",
                     "The chance depends on the missing value itself, after accounting for the model"),
  `Can the data tell?` = c("Partly: it can reject it, not confirm it",
                           "No: the missing values are the only evidence",
                           "No"),
  `A model with all the available data is` = c("Valid, and so is dropping rows (less efficient)",
                                                "Valid for the mean; dropping rows is not",
                                                "Biased; a model of the loss, or a sensitivity analysis, is needed"),
  `Where I would put the cases here` = c("A section lost to a cutting accident",
                                         "Mice that stop coming after a first session whose score is in the model",
                                         "A tracker that loses the mouse because of what the mouse does"),
  check.names = FALSE
```

Two sentences of that table carry most of what follows. The first is that **no analysis can show you that data are missing at random**, because the evidence against it sits in the values you do not have. The second is that, nevertheless, you can make the assumption *explicit and test how much the conclusion depends on it*, which is what a sensitivity analysis is. I will do the first thing for the wire, where the mechanism is known (the cap is a rule, so we know exactly what is censored), and the second for the open field, where it is not.

## Hidden behind a limit: the clock that stops at 60 seconds {#sec-mdme-wire}

Imagine a marathon in which the officials switch off the clock at four hours. You are given the finishing times and asked for the average. The runners who were still on the course are not in the list of times, and the average of the ones who finished is a number that tells you how long the race takes *for those who finish in under four hours*. It is not wrong as an arithmetic mean. It is wrong as an answer to the question that you were asked, which was about the runners, and it is wrong in a predictable direction: the slowest runners are exactly the ones that were dropped.

The wire is that marathon. @tbl-mdme_outcomes counts how the 567 attempts ended, by genotype. 9 of 252 attempts of control mice reached the cap (3.6%), against 36 of 315 of Klf4-KO mice (11.4%), and the six falls are all in the knockouts.






::: {#tbl-mdme_outcomes .cell tbl-cap='How the 567 attempts of the hanging wire test ended, by genotype. The two crossings recorded at exactly 60 seconds are counted among the crossings.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Counts and shares by genotype; the share not completed adds the cap and the falls
out_df <- data.frame(
  Genotype = c("Control", "Klf4-KO"),
  Attempts = as.integer(n_by_geno),
  Crossed = as.integer(end_tab[, "Crossed"]),
  `Reached the cap` = as.integer(end_tab[, "Reached the cap"]),
  Fell = as.integer(end_tab[, "Fell"]),
  `Not completed (%)` = round(100 * (end_tab[, "Reached the cap"] + end_tab[, "Fell"]) / as.integer(n_by_geno), 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(out_df)
```

|:--|:--------|--------:|-------:|---------------:|----:|-----------------:|
|WT |Control  |      252|     243|               9|    0|               3.6|
|KO |Klf4-KO  |      315|     273|              36|    6|              13.3|

I want the size of the problem in numbers before building anything. If I drop the failed attempts, I drop 3.6% of the attempts of controls and 13.3% of those of knockouts, which is 3.7 times as many. The knockouts have the slowest mice, and they lose the most of their slowest attempts. A comparison of what is left compares a nearly complete set of control times with a trimmed set of knockout times, so it makes the knockouts look *less* different from controls than they are. The name for this, when the chance of being censored depends on the group or on the value, is [informative censoring]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. If the cap were an administrative accident that hit attempts at random (the experimenter had to leave at attempt 4), the censoring would be harmless to the comparison and the loss would only be a loss of information. Here the cap hits slowness, and slowness is what we are measuring [@harrell2015].

The case of one mouse shows it without a model. Mouse KO86 has 7 attempts at the cap and 2 completed ones, at 25 and 23 seconds. The average of its completed attempts is 24 seconds, which describes a quick mouse. Its average over all nine attempts is *at least* 52 seconds, because every attempt at the cap would have been 60 or more. The first number is what dropping reports; the second is the truth with a floor under it. A [censored]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} observation is exactly this: a measurement that we only know to be beyond a limit. When the limit is an upper one, as the 60-second cap, the observation is [right-censored]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}; when it is a lower one, as a value below the detection limit of an assay, it is [left-censored]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. And a [truncated]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} observation is a different thing: a unit that is never in the sample at all if its value is beyond the limit, so that we do not even know it existed. Censored units are in the data with a bound; truncated units are not [@harrell2015].

We can read it up to the point where the fog begins, and after that we only know that the thing we are measuring is at least that long.](images/missing-data-measurement-error_ruler-into-fog.png){#fig-mdme-ruler fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a long wooden ruler lying on an off-white table, with clear tick marks on the left that fade into a bank of pale teal fog on the right, where the ruler is only a faint outline. A small white mouse stands at the edge of the fog, looking up into it."}

@fig-mdme-ruler is the whole idea of censoring in one picture: up to the fog the marks tell us how long the thing is, and beyond it we only know that it is at least that long.

### Every attempt, accounted for {#sec-mdme-km}

Before any model, I want a picture in which *no attempt is dropped and none is invented*. The question that fits the data is not "what was the time?" but "by second *t*, what share of the attempts had not yet been completed?". That is a [survival curve]{.ix ix="survival curve"} in the language of time-to-event analysis (the share still "surviving", here still on the wire at time *t*), estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method [@kaplan1958], and it handles a censored attempt in the only honest way: it stays in the denominator until the moment its clock stops, and leaves then. I use `survival::survfit()` [@survival] and draw the steps with `ggplot2::geom_step()` and a ribbon for the 95% confidence interval. A bar plot of mean times would give one number per genotype; this curve gives every second of the test, and it shows where the two groups separate and what is left at the end.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Time to cross: an attempt that crossed is an event; the rest leave the risk set when their clock stops
km_dat <- attempts
km_dat$time <- pmax(km_dat$wire, 0.5)
km_dat$event <- as.numeric(km_dat$end == "Crossed")
sf <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ genotype, data = km_dat)

# Steps of each curve, with the starting point at time 0
sf_df <- data.frame(time = sf$time, surv = sf$surv, lo = sf$lower, hi = sf$upper,
                    genotype = rep(c("WT", "KO"), sf$strata))
sf_df <- rbind(sf_df, data.frame(time = 0, surv = 1, lo = 1, hi = 1, genotype = c("WT", "KO")))

# Height of the curve at the moment each fall happened (the crosses)
fall_df <- attempts[attempts$end == "Fell", c("genotype", "wire")]
fall_df$surv <- NA
for (i in seq_len(nrow(fall_df))) {
  s <- sf_df[sf_df$genotype == fall_df$genotype[i], ]
  s <- s[order(s$time), ]
  fall_df$surv[i] <- tail(s$surv[s$time <= fall_df$wire[i]], 1)
}

# Share still hanging when the clock stops, for the labels on the right
end_surv <- sapply(c("WT", "KO"), function(g) min(sf_df$surv[sf_df$genotype == g]))

# Curves, ribbons, direct labels, the cap, and the falls
ggplot(sf_df, aes(x = time, y = surv, color = genotype, fill = genotype)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), stat = "identity", alpha = 0.15, colour = NA, outline.type = "full") +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(data = fall_df, aes(x = wire, y = surv), shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1.2, color = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 36, y = 0.50, label = "Klf4-KO", color = col_geno[["KO"]], fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 24, y = 0.12, label = "Control", color = col_geno[["WT"]], fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 59, y = 0.60, label = "cap", hjust = 1, size = 4.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_geno) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_geno) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 62)) +
  labs(x = "Time on the wire (s)", y = "Share of attempts not yet completed") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none()
```

I read the picture in three steps, and this is how I would teach you to read any curve of this kind.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
The vertical axis is the share of attempts still *not completed* at the second on the horizontal axis, so every curve starts at 1 and can only go down. First look at how fast each curve falls: a curve that falls early is a group that crosses quickly. Then look at the height of the curve at the dotted line. That height is the share of attempts that were still hanging when the clock stopped, which is the censored share, and here it is 3.6% for controls and 12% for knockouts. Last, notice that the curves are flat after 60: the test says nothing about what would have happened, so the flat part is not a prediction. The mistake to avoid is to read the plateau as "these mice never cross"; it says "we stopped looking".
:::

The two curves tell the story of the chapter before I fit anything. The knockouts' curve is above the controls' at every second, which is what a slower group looks like, and it ends at a plateau about 3.3 times as high. The model I build next is a way of putting that picture into one number (a ratio of typical crossing times) *without* throwing away the attempts that make the plateau.

### Two things that are not censored times {#sec-mdme-falls}

Two groups of attempts need a decision before the model, and I made the rule first and checked it in code, as I did with the impossible record in @sec-beta-robust-regression. The first group is the six **falls**. A mouse that falls at 12 seconds has not been stopped by the cap. It has had a different event, and what its "time to cross" would have been had it stayed on is a counterfactual that I do not know how to fill in; it is not "at least 12 seconds" in the way that a timeout is "at least 60", because falling may itself be related to how hard the crossing was. All six are in knockout mice, on days 1 to 3 (@tbl-mdme_falls).






::: {#tbl-mdme_falls .cell tbl-cap='The six attempts that ended in a fall before the cap, and the two crossings recorded at exactly 60 seconds. Times in seconds; position is the time to get into position.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
odd$end <- ifelse(odd$end == "Fell", "Fell", "Crossed at exactly 60 s")
names(odd) <- c("Mouse", "Genotype", "Day", "Attempt", "Position", "Time", "How it ended")
knitr::kable(odd[order(odd$`How it ended`, odd$Mouse), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

My rule for the main analysis is therefore: **falls are not censored times, and they are left out of the model of the crossing time**; they are counted, reported (6 of 315 attempts of knockouts, none in controls), and shown with their own sensitivity analysis below, in which they are treated in the two ways that bracket the possibilities. The second group is the two crossings recorded at exactly 60 seconds. Daniel confirmed that these mice reached the platform in the last second, so they are real crossings and I keep them as exact times of 60 s; the cost of being wrong is small and I tested it, by refitting with both of them recoded as censored. They are the kind of boundary case that is only visible because I looked for values that sit on a limit.

### The censored model {#sec-mdme-censmodel}

The model is the Student-*t* of @sec-beta-robust-regression on the log of the time, with the varying intercept for each mouse of @sec-multilevel-glmm, and one change in the likelihood. For an attempt that was completed, the likelihood contribution is the height of the density at the observed log time, as always. For an attempt that reached the cap, I do not have a log time; what I have is that the log time was *larger than* $\log 60$, and the contribution is the probability of that, the area under the density beyond the cap (@eq-mdme-cens). The mouse that hit the cap contributes less than a mouse that crossed, because it tells us less, but it contributes in the right direction.

$$
L_i = \begin{cases}
f\left(\log y_i \mid \mu_i, \sigma, \nu\right) & \text{if the attempt was completed}\\[4pt]
1 - F\left(\log 60 \mid \mu_i, \sigma, \nu\right) & \text{if it reached the cap}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-mdme-cens}

with $f$ and $F$ the density and the cumulative distribution function of the Student-*t* and $\mu_i$ the linear predictor of @sec-multilevel-glmm: genotype, day and attempt, plus a level for the mouse. In `brms` the only change is the left side of the formula: `log_wire | cens(cens)`, where `cens` says for each row whether the value is exact (`"none"`) or a lower bound (`"right"`). The priors are those of @sec-multilevel-glmm (`Normal(3, 0.7)` for the intercept on the log scale, `Normal(0, 0.5)` for coefficients, `Exponential(2)` for the scale, `Gamma(2, 0.1)` for the degrees of freedom and `Exponential(3)` for the spread between mice), so that the *only* thing that changes is what I do with the censored attempts. I fit that model and the alternatives that I want to compare it with: the Gaussian of the first chapter on behavior (completed attempts, independent), the Student-*t* with a level for mouse on completed attempts only (the model of @sec-multilevel-glmm), and the Student-*t* in which the capped attempts are entered as exact times of 60 seconds (the replacement that I warned you about).

@fig-mdme_wire_forest has one message and one caution. The message: **dropping the capped attempts makes the knockout delay look smaller** (a ratio of 1.27 [1.17, 1.38] with the Gaussian of the chapter on behavior and 1.28 [1.08, 1.51] with the Student-*t* on completed attempts with a level for each mouse), the replacement gets closer (1.40 [1.13, 1.71]), since a 60 is at least a lower bound of the truth, but it invents a value and gives it the weight of a measurement, and the censored model says 1.44 [1.13, 1.80]: the typical crossing of a knockout takes 44% longer than that of a control, not 28%. The direction is the one I predicted from @tbl-mdme_outcomes. The caution is about *how much*: the censored interval is wider than the interval of the models that dropped attempts, and it should be, because it admits that 45 of the attempts told us only a bound. A narrower interval from a model that discards the hardest attempts is not a better result; it is a more confident answer to an easier question.

Three sensitivity analyses sit below the main row. The two about the falls bracket what a fall could mean: if a fall is just "we stopped watching" the ratio is 1.44 [1.14, 1.81], and if a fall is as bad as reaching the cap (every mouse that fell would have hung on until the end) it is 1.45 [1.15, 1.84]. Six attempts out of 567 do not decide the conclusion, and the figure says so. Recoding the two crossings at exactly 60 seconds as censored gives 1.43 [1.13, 1.78]. And the frequentist estimate from `survival::survreg()` is 1.41 (95% confidence interval 1.14 to 1.74).

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`survreg()` fits the censored model by maximum likelihood, with a lognormal distribution for the time (a Gaussian on the log scale) instead of the Student-*t*, and with standard errors that allow for the clustering of attempts within mice (`cluster(mouse)`). That is not the same model as the `brms` one: it has no varying intercept, so the mouse-to-mouse variation enters only through the standard error, and its tails are those of a Gaussian. The agreement of the point estimate with the censored `brms` model (1.41 against 1.44) is the reassuring part: the censored likelihood is doing the work, in both. Where they differ is in the width of the interval and in how they treat mice: `brms` estimates the spread between mice and shrinks each mouse toward its genotype; `survreg()` ignores that structure and corrects the standard error afterwards. `parsnip`, which the book used for the simple models, has no engine for a censored regression with a varying intercept, and `survreg()` in `survival` does not support random effects (I tried a Gaussian frailty term and it is refused). A Cox model with a random intercept exists in the `coxme` package, but it answers a different question (a ratio of hazards, not of times) and belongs to the appendix on time-to-event models (@sec-appendix-next), which I do not enter.
:::

### The other view: the probability of not completing {#sec-mdme-logit}

Everything so far is about *how long* a crossing takes. The other question the data can answer is *whether* it happens, and it is the one that does not need any assumption about the values behind the cap. I model the probability that an attempt is not completed (reaches the cap or falls) with the logistic model with a varying intercept of @sec-multilevel-glmm, and I report it two ways, as an odds ratio for a typical mouse and as the average difference in probability over the mice we studied (@sec-glmm-marginal).






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Not completed (cap or fall) as a yes/no, with a level for each mouse
attempts$failed <- 1 - attempts$success
fit_w10 <- brm(
  failed ~ genotype + day_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = attempts, family = bernoulli(), prior = prior_logit,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit10.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
dr_l <- as_draws_df(fit_w10)

# Average predictive comparison: every attempt as if by a knockout and as if by a control
nd_ko <- attempts; nd_ko$genotype <- factor("KO", levels = c("WT", "KO"))
nd_wt <- attempts; nd_wt$genotype <- factor("WT", levels = c("WT", "KO"))
p_ko <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit_w10, newdata = nd_ko))
p_wt <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit_w10, newdata = nd_wt))
```
:::






For a typical mouse the odds of not completing an attempt are 5.4 [1.2, 25.8] times as large in knockouts as in controls; averaged over the mice of the experiment, the probability of not completing an attempt is 12.3 [8.6, 17.1]% for knockouts against 4.1 [1.9, 8.7]% for controls, a difference of 8.1 [0.9, 14.3] percentage points. This view and the censored model agree about the direction and about the group that is in trouble, and they do so for different reasons: the logistic model uses only whether the attempt ended at all, and the censored model uses *also* how close to the cap the completed attempts were. Reporting both is not redundancy. A reader who distrusts the tail assumption of the censored model can fall back on the probability, and a reader who wants the time can have it.

### Does the censored model reproduce the cap? {#sec-mdme-ppc}

A model for a limit should, at the least, reproduce *how often the limit is reached*. I check it by simulating, from the censored model, a new time for every attempt and counting how often the simulated time is above 60 seconds, by genotype and day, against the observed share of attempts at the cap (@fig-mdme_wire_ppc). It is the predictive check of @sec-mcmc-model-checking, with a statistic chosen for the problem: the share beyond the cap, because the cap is exactly what this chapter is about.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** Of 567 attempts by 63 mice, 9 of 252 attempts of control mice and 36 of 315 of Klf4-KO mice reached the 60-second limit of the test, and 6 attempts, all by knockouts, ended in a fall. Treating the limit as a right-censored time, the typical crossing time of Klf4-KO mice was 1.44 [1.13, 1.80] times that of controls (posterior median and 95% credible interval; a posterior probability above 99% that the ratio exceeds 1), against 1.28 [1.08, 1.51] when the capped attempts were omitted. Each day of training reduced crossing times by a factor of 0.80 [0.77, 0.84]. The probability of not completing an attempt was 12.3 [8.6, 17.1]% in knockouts and 4.1 [1.9, 8.7]% in controls, and it did not fall with training in knockouts, which the time model does not reproduce.

**Methods.** The log of the time on the wire was modeled with a Student-*t* likelihood, with genotype, day and attempt as predictors and a varying intercept for each mouse. Attempts that reached the 60-second limit were treated as right-censored at 60 s; falls (6 attempts) were excluded from the time model and analyzed in sensitivity analyses in which they were censored at the time of the fall or treated as reaching the limit. The model was fitted in `brms` (four chains of 3,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). The estimate assumes that the log times beyond 60 s follow the same Student-*t* distribution as the observed ones; the model under-predicted the share of attempts at the limit on days 2 and 3.
:::

## Absent: sessions and sections that are not there {#sec-mdme-absent}

The wire was the easy case, in one sense: the mechanism is a rule that I can read in the lab manual, so I know exactly which values are censored and by how much. The absent values of the rest of this part are harder, because nobody wrote a rule for them. A tracker loses a mouse; a section is damaged on the cryostat; an animal does not wake up from the surgery. For each of them I can ask three questions, and the order matters: *what is missing, why do I think it is missing, and what would change my mind?*

### The open-field sessions that the tracker lost {#sec-mdme-of}

The open-field data are those of @sec-beta-robust-regression and @sec-longitudinal-timeseries, and I do not reopen any of their decisions: the animal is identified by the `Animal` column, animals whose treatment label changes between days are left out, the outcome is the share of the *tracked* time spent in the center, and a session needs at least 270 of its 300 seconds tracked. The rule of 270 seconds was inherited, not chosen, and the chapter on longitudinal models refit the model without it and said that the conclusion did not depend on where the line was drawn. Here I want to look at *what the rule removed*.

#### A sensitivity analysis for what nobody can see {#sec-mdme-tipping}

For the sessions that the tracker lost I cannot assume anything I can check, so I do the other thing the books recommend: I make the assumption a number and move the number. This is a [tipping-point analysis]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, a form of delta adjustment [@gelman2020; @harrell2015]: assume that the lost sessions differ from the kept ones by an amount $\delta$ on the log-odds scale of the center share, recompute the conclusion for each $\delta$, and look for the $\delta$ at which the conclusion changes (tips). It is the analogue of asking a reviewer "how wrong would my assumption have to be for you to stop believing this?", and the answer is the thing to report.

The conclusion that I test is the jump of day 1: the difference in the mean share of time in the center between ischemic and sham animals, averaged over the two genotypes. I fit it on the kept sessions of day 1 with a zero-inflated beta likelihood, as in the earlier chapters, and a precision for each group, because the sham animals are far less variable than the ischemic ones. Then I add the lost sessions *back by assumption*. If a share $\pi_g$ of the day-1 sessions of group $g$ is lost, and the lost ones have a mean center share $\mu_g^{lost}$ whose log-odds differ from the kept ones by $\delta$, the mean of the whole group is a weighted average (@eq-mdme-delta). With $\delta = 0$ the lost sessions are like the kept ones (missing at random within the group); a negative $\delta$ says that the tracker lost mice that spent less time in the center.

$$
\mu_g(\delta) = (1 - \pi_g)\,\mu_g^{kept} + \pi_g\,\text{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\text{logit}(\mu_g^{kept}) + \delta\right)
$$ {#eq-mdme-delta}






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nd_g <- data.frame(group = factor(levels(d1$group), levels = levels(d1$group)))

# Share of the day-1 sessions that were lost, by group
pi_lost <- as.numeric(tapply(d1$short, d1$group, mean))

# The group means after adding the lost sessions with a shift delta on the logit scale (equation above)
adj_means <- function(m, delta) {
  out <- m
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(m))) out[, j] <- (1 - pi_lost[j]) * m[, j] + pi_lost[j] * plogis(qlogis(m[, j]) + delta)
  out
}

# The conclusion: mean share of ischemic animals minus that of shams (percentage points), over genotypes
jump_fun <- function(m) 100 * (rowMeans(m[, c(2, 4)]) - rowMeans(m[, c(1, 3)]))

# A grid of deltas; -Inf is the extreme in which every lost session had no time in the center at all
delta_grid <- c(-Inf, seq(-6, 3, by = 0.5))

  q <- quantile(jump_fun(adj_means(m_kept, d)), c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975, 0.25, 0.75))
  data.frame(delta = d, med = q[1], lo = q[2], hi = q[3], lo50 = q[4], hi50 = q[5])
}))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
The horizontal axis is an assumption, not a measurement: how different the sessions that the tracker lost were from the ones it kept, with 0 meaning "not different" and negative values meaning "they spent less time in the center". The vertical axis is the conclusion. Read the line from the 0 to the left, which is the direction that the data suggest, and ask whether the band ever touches the dashed line at zero. If it does, the position of that crossing is the *tipping point*, and the question to ask is whether such an assumption is plausible. If the band never touches it, the conclusion does not depend on the assumption, within the range that you drew. The mistake to avoid is to read the figure as saying that the assumption is true: it says how much it would have to be false for the answer to change.
:::

The conclusion about the jump does not tip. The lower limit of the interval stays above zero across the whole range, down to the extreme case in which every lost session had no time in the center, and the reason is arithmetic that you can check by hand (@eq-mdme-delta): only 22% of the ischemic sessions of day 1 were lost, so even if every one of them had a center share of zero, the mean of the ischemic groups could fall by at most that share of what it was. What *does* change is the size of the jump, from 14.5 percentage points to 11 at the extreme, which says that the inherited rule makes the jump look larger than it is, in the direction that @fig-mdme_of_lost suggested, but not by enough to reverse it. That is the form that a result about missing data should take: not "the data are missing at random", which I cannot know, but "the conclusion holds for every shift I can think of, and the size depends on it as follows".

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`glmmTMB` (@brooks2017) fits the same zero-inflated beta by maximum likelihood, and the group means that it reports agree with the posterior medians of `brms`, as they should with a day-1 sample of 38 animals and weak priors. What the frequentist fit cannot do is the next step: a tipping-point analysis is a calculation on the *estimated* means, so I can run it on the maximum-likelihood estimates as well, but there is no distribution of the jump to carry the uncertainty through unless I resample (bootstrap) the animals. The Bayesian fit gives that distribution for free, which is the practical reason why the book keeps `brms` first in a sensitivity analysis. A frequentist counterpart of the *reasoning* is a pattern-mixture model fitted by hand, which is the equation above; the textbooks present it as the standard way to examine data that are missing not at random [@harrell2015].
:::

In a tipping-point analysis, the 95% interval of the difference excluded zero for every shift in the log-odds of the center share of the excluded sessions between minus infinity (no time in the center) and 3; the difference was 12.0 [4.8, 19.1] percentage points with the shift suggested by the partially tracked sessions (-1.6) and 11.0 [4.5, 17.6] in the extreme case.

**Methods.** The share of the tracked time in the center was modeled with a zero-inflated beta likelihood, with a mean and a precision for each of four groups (genotype by surgery) in `brms` (four chains of 2,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). Excluded sessions were added to the group means by assumption, with a shift $\delta$ on the logit scale (pattern-mixture; equation above). Loss of sessions after day 1 (4 animals, attributed to postoperative mortality) was not modeled.

## Blurred: a count has an error bar that the spreadsheet does not show {#sec-mdme-blurred}

The third jar is the one that scientists forget to open, because nothing in the file says it is there. A NeuN density is a count of positive cells divided by the area of a region, and a count made by a microscope and a counting rule is a *sample* of the cells in the tissue: if I could cut the same section again and count again, I would not get the same number. The [counting error]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} of a count is known, to a good approximation, and that is what makes it a clean case of [measurement error]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: for a Poisson count of $n$ cells the standard deviation is $\sqrt{n}$, so the *relative* error is $1/\sqrt{n}$. A thousand cells give an error of about 3%; a hundred give 10%; ten give 32%. The question is not whether it exists, but *whether it is big enough to matter*, and the way to answer it is to put it next to the spread that you care about.

I do that in @fig-mdme_counting for every structure of the NeuN experiment. For each section I plot the relative counting error of its count (`1 / sqrt(count)`) and next to it, as a black bar, the standard deviation of the log density between sections of the same day and hemisphere, which is the biological and technical variation that the model of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts is about. Both are on the same scale (a proportion of the density), so a point below the bar is a count whose error is smaller than the spread between sections.








::: {.cell}

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read it in two steps. First compare each cloud of points with the bar in its own column: if the cloud is far below the bar, the counting error is small next to the variation between sections and a model that treats the count as exact loses almost nothing. Second look for the points that climb toward the bar: those are the sections with few cells, the ones where the count is the weakest evidence. The mistake to avoid is to read a small counting error as a statement that the *density* is precise: it says that the count is a good sample of the tissue that was counted, and nothing about whether the section is typical of the animal.
:::

The result is a finding, not a failure: **in this experiment the counting error is small next to the biology.** In the cortex the median relative error is 1.1% against a spread between sections of 36%, and even in the structures with the smallest counts, the fiber tracts, the median error is 3.6% against a spread of 53%. In variance terms, which is what a model sees, the counting error accounts for about 0.1% of the variance of the cortex and 1.2% of that of the fiber tracts. A rule that I find useful is to compare the average of $1/n$ with the variance of the log density you are modeling: when the first is below a few percent of the second, the error does not matter for the mean. The books agree on the principle: the rate is a latent quantity, and treating a ratio of counts as if it were known matters when counts are small or when the exposure (here, the area) varies a lot between units, and it can be ignored when the biological variation is much larger than the counting noise [@mcelreath2020].

Where does the counting error matter, then? Where there are few cells. The fiber tracts, the cerebral nuclei, the interbrain and the midbrain have 63 regions with fewer than 100 positive cells (@tbl-mdme_error_share), with relative errors of 10% or more, and the smallest regions are slivers at the edge of a section. In those, a model that treats the density as exact gives a count of 20 the same weight as a count of 2,000, which is the problem that the books name: a ratio of counts is a rate with a precision that depends on the denominator [@mcelreath2020]. There are two ways to give the model what it needs, and I show both on the fiber tracts, which are the structure with the most small counts.

The first is to keep the log density as the outcome and tell the model *how precisely each one is known*. In `brms` the term `se(sei, sigma = TRUE)` on the left of the formula says that each observation has a known standard error `sei`, here $1/\sqrt{n}$, on the log scale, and that there is, in addition, a residual spread `sigma` to be estimated (the variation between sections that is *not* the counting error). The second is to model the counts themselves, with the log of the area as an offset and a negative binomial likelihood, which is what @sec-count-regression and @sec-multilevel-glmm did: a count model carries the Poisson error automatically, because the variance of a count is part of its distribution, and a region with zero cells stays in (there are five in the cerebral nuclei and the midbrain, none in the fiber tracts), which the log density cannot do.

#### The distribution of the measurement error is also a model {#sec-mdme-sigma}

The chapter on distributional regression promised that the variance of the *measurement* would become one more thing to model (@sec-multivariate-distributional-regression), and the `se()` term is where that promise is kept. ### An error in a predictor is a different problem {#sec-mdme-me}

What I have described is measurement error in an *outcome*, and the books are clear that it is the benign case: noise in $y$ folds into the residual, it widens the intervals and it does not bias the slope [@gelman2020; @mcelreath2020]. Noise in a *predictor* is not benign, because it pulls the slope toward zero (attenuation): if you regress a response on a noisy version of $x$, a part of the variation of $x_{obs}$ is noise that has nothing to do with the response, and the slope is diluted by the share of the variance of $x_{obs}$ that is true signal (the *reliability*). In `brms` the term is `me(x, sdx)`, which declares a latent true $x$ with the observed one distributed around it with the known standard deviation `sdx`.

I have a real case in the data that I already know, and I run it in order to see what happens, not to find an effect. In `cell_data` the number of PDGFR-β+ cells (`Pdgfrb_Pos`) is a count, with a Poisson counting error, and the question can be: *at the same day, do animals with more PDGFR-β+ cells have a higher GFAP integrated density?* The predictor is the count (on the log scale, with an error of $1/\sqrt{n}$) and the outcome is the log of the GFAP integrated density.






::: {.cell}


### Values below a limit of detection, which I can explain but not demonstrate {#sec-mdme-lod}

The first-class case of a hidden value on the *low* side is a measurement below the limit of detection of an assay: an ELISA concentration below the lowest standard, a band too faint on the film, a qPCR reaction whose Ct is "undetermined". The practice that I see most often is to replace the value by half the limit (or by the limit divided by $\sqrt{2}$) and carry on. The books that this one follows are of one voice against it: it creates a spike of identical values that did not exist, shrinks the spread, and distorts the slopes and the correlations [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. The alternative is the one that you already know from the wire: a [left-censored]{.ix ix="left-censored"} observation is a value that is *at most* the limit, and it contributes to the likelihood the probability of being below it, $F(\text{limit}\mid\mu,\sigma)$. In `brms` the only change is the left side of the formula, and `cens = "left"`.

## An NA, a zero and a value below detection {#sec-mdme-td79}

I left for the end a case that I find the best teaching example in the book, because it is a single animal. In @sec-eda-missing-data I met animal `Td79` (three days after ischemia) because its `Pdgfrb_Neg` is missing, and I showed that its `Pdgfrb_Total` equals its `Pdgfrb_Pos` (398), which means that whoever computed the total treated the missing count as zero. There are two more things in that row. Its `PdgfrbLow_Intensity` is exactly 0, the only zero of that column. And the value that is missing is a *count of negative cells*, which is something that can be zero.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The rule that the file obeys everywhere else: positives plus negatives equal the total
chk_neg <- cell_data[!is.na(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg), ]
rule_holds <- all(chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Pos + chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Neg == chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Total)

# A DECISION, CONFIRMED AS A WORKING READING BY DANIEL: the negatives are the total minus the positives,
# which is zero for Td79 (it has no PDGFR-beta-negative cells)
cell_data$neg_rec <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_Total - cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos
cell_data$neg_100 <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg / 100
cell_data$neg_rec_100 <- cell_data$neg_rec / 100
td <- cell_data[cell_data$MouseID == "Td79", ]
stopifnot(rule_holds, td$neg_rec == 0, sum(is.na(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg)) == 1)
others_d3 <- cell_data[cell_data$DPI == 3 & cell_data$MouseID != "Td79", ]
```
:::






The rule `Pos + Neg = Total` holds in all of the 48 animals with a recorded `Pdgfrb_Neg`. For `Td79`, applying it backwards gives `Pdgfrb_Neg` equal to 0, which is a very specific claim: *this animal has no PDGFR-β-negative cells in the section*. I asked, and the answer is that it may very well be the case. I take it as a working reading, not as a fact, and I say why it is not obviously safe: the other 7 animals of the same day have between 63 and 537 negative cells, and no animal in the whole file has fewer than 63. A section with 398 positive cells and none negative would be an unusual section, and it is worth checking on the image. Under that reading, the `NA` is not missing at all: it is a *structural* value that can be reconstructed from the other columns, and nobody should impute it. Under the other reading (the negatives were not counted, and the total is wrong), it is a missing count, and the imputation of @sec-eda-missing-data is the right treatment. The data cannot tell the two apart; the images can.

Then there is the intensity. `PdgfrbLow_Intensity` is 0 for `Td79`, and it is the only zero in a column whose other values go from 2.5 to 51. It is tempting to read it as a measurement below a detection limit (a very faint signal), and it is not: the column is the intensity of the "low" class of PDGFR-β, and if that class has no cells there is nothing to measure. A zero here is not a faint value. It is, at best, a sum over an empty set, and at worst an undefined mean, written as zero by a script that did not know what else to write. ## Missing predictors, and imputation as estimation {#sec-mdme-predictors}

The animal `Td79` was a missing *predictor*, and a missing predictor is the case in which the machinery of imputation earns its keep, because a model cannot simply drop what it needs to condition on without paying in rows. The idea that this chapter adds to @sec-eda-missing-data is a change of what we call it. In the Bayesian framework a missing value is not a hole to be filled before the analysis, it is an **unknown, and an unknown is a parameter**: it gets a prior (here, a sub-model for the variable that has gaps) and a posterior, estimated jointly with everything else [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. The imputed values are then not "data" that the analysis treats as known, they carry their uncertainty into every other parameter, and that is the whole difference with plugging in a mean.

The practical comparison with multiple imputation is shorter than it sounds. Multiple imputation (`mice`) draws several completed datasets from a model for the variable with gaps, fits the analysis on each, and pools with Rubin's rules [@mice]; `mi()` does the draw at every iteration of the sampler, inside the model. Both assume the loss is missing at random given what is in the imputation model, and the pitfall that I will repeat because it is the commonest one is that **the imputation model must include the outcome**: a model that imputes $x$ without looking at $y$ is assuming that they are unrelated, and it flattens the slope toward zero [@harrell2015; @mcelreath2020]. Both of mine did include it (the `mice` call has `log_pos` in the data, and `mi()` is fitted jointly with the outcome).

When there are *many* missing values in several predictors, which I do not have in the book, the syntax grows to one sub-model per incomplete variable. I show it in a chunk that is not run, with invented names, so that you can see the shape of it, and I would be glad to replace it with a real dataset if you have one with missing covariates.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# ILLUSTRATION, NOT RUN: two incomplete predictors, each with its own sub-model (invented names).
# Every row keeps its place; the missing x1 and x2 are estimated as parameters, jointly with the outcome
brm(
  bf(y ~ mi(x1) + mi(x2) + group + (1 | animal)) +
    bf(x1 | mi() ~ group) +
    bf(x2 | mi() ~ group + mi(x1)) +
    set_rescor(FALSE),
  data = dat, family = gaussian()
)
```
:::






`mi()` works only with continuous variables, because Stan cannot sample discrete parameters, so a missing count has to be handled as continuous or integrated out [@mcelreath2020], and when the loss is not at random the sub-model has to be extended with a model of the missingness itself, or replaced by a sensitivity analysis as in @sec-mdme-tipping.

## What to write in a paper {#sec-mdme-report}

Three of the "How to report it" blocks above are the ones I would paste into a Results section: the censored comparison of crossing times, the tipping-point analysis of the open field, and the animal whose value was reconstructed. There is a fourth sentence that is easy to forget, and it is the one that a reviewer is most likely to want: *what was missing, why, and what was assumed*. I would put it in Methods, once, for the whole study.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Methods.** Of 567 attempts on the hanging wire, 45 reached the 60-second limit and were treated as right-censored, and 6 ended in a fall and were analyzed separately. Of 275 open-field sessions in the 48 animals analyzed, 29 had fewer than 270 s of tracking; they were excluded from the main analysis and examined in a sensitivity analysis on the log-odds scale of the center share, and 4 animals had no session after day 1 or day 15 (attributed to postoperative mortality). For the NeuN counts, 15 sections after the sixth were not available for 15 mice and 4 sections were lost inside a series; the comparison of hemispheres was unchanged when they were excluded. Counting error (Poisson) accounted for less than 7% of the variance between sections in every structure. Missing data were assumed to be missing at random given the group, the day and the animal's earlier values, except where a sensitivity analysis is reported.
:::

## What the chapter leaves behind {#sec-mdme-close}

We started with three mice at 60 seconds and a question, and what I hope you take is a habit more than a model. Before touching any code, ask which of three things has happened: the value is *absent*, *hidden behind a limit* or *blurred*. An absent value asks for a reason and an honest statement of what the analysis assumes, and, when the assumption cannot be checked, a sensitivity analysis that turns it into a number you can move. A hidden value asks to stay in the model with what we know about it, which is that it is beyond a limit, instead of being dropped, replaced by the limit or replaced by half of it. A blurred value asks to be put next to the variation that matters and, if it is not negligible, to be carried by the model. And a zero, an NA and a value below detection are three different things, which a single animal in a table of 49 was enough to show.

The result about the wire was that dropping the capped attempts made the knockout delay look about 16 percentage points smaller than the censored model says, and the open-field result was that the inherited rule makes the day-1 jump look larger than it is, by an amount that does not reverse it. Two small things in opposite directions, from the same cause, which is that the values that are easiest to lose are the ones that matter. The books I have used agree on this: the question is never whether to take the missing values seriously, but which of the three jars they come from [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020; @harrell2015].

Two topics are left outside on purpose. The first is time-to-event analysis proper, with hazards, competing risks and frailty models, which is the natural next step from the Kaplan-Meier curve of @fig-mdme_km and has its own place in the appendix on what comes next (@sec-appendix-next). The second is the question of what a statistic *means* when the cause of the missing values is part of the story, which is what the next chapter, @sec-causal-inference-splines, takes up with the tools of causal inference: a diagram of what causes the loss is exactly what tells you whether the loss is ignorable.
